  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint off with a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/inness_materials.md (his materials and method) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

events.out:
nd a failed chunk
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** Masks and forms are large: keep big ones `local` when
  later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard

46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

  of sold and exhibited works, including scraping with a palette knife
  when the underlying paint was still too wet to rub off. X-radiography confirms major revisions.

## 8. Condition and aging

- **Traction crackle.** "Traction crackle is found in thicker areas of
  brown paint". On one repainted canvas, bitumen or a resin
  addition "probably also caused the considerable traction crackle and
  'crawl' of paint".
- **Abrasion or scraping.** On one canvas "it is difficult to determine
  what is the result of damage and what was intentional scraping by the
  artist during repainting".
- **Cleaning risk.** Restorers in the 1930s damaged one of his canvases
  when they removed his own retouching, mistaking it for old restoration. A well-preserved surface is "somewhat unusual for Inness' work".
- **Old paint showing through.** Cracks in an early canvas reveal a lower
  paint layer.

## 9. The tubes here

The historical names in this note correspond to these tubes: white →
lead white (assumed); black and ivory black → bone black; yellow ocher → yellow
ochre; umber → raw umber; sienna → raw sienna; cadmium → cadmium yellow;
Venetian red → red earth.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with ground layers laid from the tubes.
- **Paint.** Pigment from the tubes with an oil-medium share.
- **Taking paint off.** A brush picks up wet paint as it passes; that is
  how paint comes off the canvas.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

events.text:
First I should check for any existing journal or notes. Now I'm sketching out a late Inness-style landscape—tonalist, soft-edged, misty light at dawn or dusk, sparse trees, maybe a lone figure, a pastoral meadow under a warm glowing sky with unified tones, drawing on works like "Home of the Heron," "Sunset in the Woods," and "Early Moon" for reference.

I'm settling on an "Evening, Montclair" composition: a dusky meadow with a central tree mass and slender trees, a low sun glowing behind them, a small figure giving a single red accent, a reflective pool, and hazy distant hills, sized at 30x45 inches (1140mm wide, 1.5 aspect ratio). For the ground, I'm leaning toward a warm red earth or raw umber stain over a lead white base so that warmth glows through the paint layers, as in Inness's late work.

I'm weighing whether to thin the raw umber with lead white for a lighter brown, or use raw sienna with a touch of umber instead, but I only get one shot at committing the ground layer so I need to choose carefully. I'm refining the composition further — thinking of calling it something like "The Close of Day, Pompton" or "October Afternoon," with a wide 1000x667 canvas, a low horizon around 63% down, and a warm glowing sky near the horizon that cools toward the top.

Now I'm placing the main elements: a dark mass of oaks or elms on the left, a slender young tree pair to the right of center against the glow, soft blue-gray hills far off along the horizon, a sunlit meadow with a shadow band in the foreground, and maybe a small figure in a red shawl walking a path to give the scene life, in Inness's characteristic manner.

I'm mapping the light structure—a glowing sky, dark trees silhouetted against it, a midtone meadow with a sunstruck patch, and a dark scrubbed foreground, with a pool reflecting the sky glow in the lower right. The palette stays late-Inness: olive greens, warm golds, rose-violet sky tones, blue grays, with that single red accent on the figure, and I start sketching out the process—prepping a linen canvas with a lead white ground and a warm stain.

Now I'm debating the stain mix for that ground, weighing raw sienna, raw umber, and red earth against lead white to get a thin, warm, luminous tint without going chalky or opaque, and wondering if I should test the ground before committing fully.

Shifting to the painting process: I'm thinking of a light chalk drawing for the horizon and tree masses, then a thin raw umber lay-in rubbed for darks with lights wiped out for the sky, followed by a sky built from lead white, yellow ochre, and red earth near the horizon cooling upward with cobalt and black, blended smoothly, before moving into the distant hills.

Continuing the plan, I'm mapping out mid-dark olive trees stippled softly into the sky, a warm yellow-green meadow with a lemon chrome highlight, sky-toned reflections in the pool, and finishing details like figures, tree gaps, and trunks with a rigger brush, then warming the foreground with glazes and scumbles once dry. First I should check whether the journal already exists.
I'll start by jotting down the plan in the journal first.

This tree mass came out too opaque and lumpy, a heavy dark blob rather than the transparent layer I wanted since the raw umber is well-loaded and hiding too much. But since it's still wet, I can lift and rub it back like Inness did, scrubbing and wiping with a rag to pull out lights before it sets.

The dome-like silhouette isn't right either—too solid and haystack-shaped, though Inness himself favored rounded masses like big elms. I'll soften the edges now by blending over the shape with a slightly grown mask, lifting paint to break it up, then let the sky paint later cut into the edge to carve out trunks and branch separations. For now I just want to fuse these dabby strokes into a softer, thinner wash.

events.text:
The unclipped blend left dark streaks radiating from the tree mass, which worries me a bit since the sky layer will be opaque lead white but those smears could still bleed through and muddy it—though that might actually read as one of Inness's characteristic underlayers showing through.

I'm weighing whether to lift the darkest streaks with a clean brush before proceeding, or simply let the lay-in dry fully before painting the sky over it so the colors don't mix wet-into-wet. Given Inness's method of working in separate campaigns, letting this transparent lay-in set first seems like the right approach.

Actually blending alone risks pushing paint around instead of removing it, so I'll loop over points along the ring and use short wiped flat-brush strokes angled radially from the tree center, wiping the brush clean after each pass to actually lift paint rather than smear it.

events.name: paint
events.code:
local ring = treeM:grow(140) - treeM:grow(4):soften(4)
local rag = brush{kind="flat", width=16, stiffness=0.6}
local n = 0
for i = 1, 500 do
  local x, y = rand(0, 650), rand(0, 520)
  if ring:at(x, y) > 0.5 then
    local a = math.atan(y - 280, x - 260)
    local dx, dy = math.cos(a), math.sin(a)
    rag:wipe(1)
    rag:stroke({{x - 30 * dx, y - 30 * dy}, {x + 30 * dx, y + 30 * dy}}, {pressure={0.7, 0.6}, orient="across"})
    n = n + 1
  end
end
print(n, wait(0))

Looking at Inness's work, the tree silhouette should be irregular and feathery with the top dissolving, something I can build with opaque layers later. The holes look too clean-edged and the gap underneath too bright and opaque against the surrounding sky, which breaks the illusion. This mask-and-fill method feels too stiff and cut-out—I need to work more painterly, dragging and scumbling to lose those hard edges, and reconsider the whole tree structure starting with the dark crown on top.

Looking at Inness references like "The Home of the Heron" and "Summer, Montclair," I think the silhouette needs irregular lobes and a visible trunk with a gap between trees rather than one bushy mass. I'm planning to repaint this as two separate trees—a tall elm on the left and a rounder oak on the right—with the space between showing distant meadow and sky glow, covering the dry paint with opaque sky color where needed before reworking the foliage edges with stippling.

I need to repaint sky over the gaps I'm opening beneath and between the crowns, but the sky color shifts across bands — blue-gray up top, pinkish-gray mid-height, pale yellow lower down — so I'll scumble matching tones into just those regions while wet. Alternatively, I could keep more of the tree mass intact and just darken trunks against a lighter distant meadow instead of opening up full sky gaps.

Thinking through Inness's late works like "Summer Evening, Montclair," "The Clouded Sun," and "Home of the Heron" for reference, I'm settling on a moderate restructuring: open the canopy at left so trunks read clearly, add a band of distant blue-gray tree line near the horizon with glimpses of sky glow above it, and break up the silhouette along the top edge.

I also want to make the crown less dome-shaped with branch clusters projecting outward and a deep sky-gap between two crown masses, while repainting the sky itself with warmer, more atmospheric variety — violet-gray clouds, a glowing break right-of-center, a heavy cloud mass low-left, and warmer sky tones near the tree edges so the foliage feels like it's breathing. I'll tackle this in stages, starting with the sky.

I'm planning to repaint the sky wet, then stipple the tree edges into the wet paint so they fuse with soft, lost edges, Inness-style. I'm mapping out the color zones from top to bottom: cooler violet-gray near the top, a warm rose-gray cloud bank in the middle, and a glowing cream-to-orange zone lower down with its brightest point just right of center.

Now I'm working out the mask logic for where sky repaint should happen — essentially everywhere above the horizon except the tree silhouette, but carving in a few small openings through the canopy so light breaks through on the lower left side of the tree.

Rather than fully opening gaps in the lower shrubbery mass, I'll just darken it and simplify it to a few key notches, since getting the top dome silhouette irregular and correct matters more for the overall shape.

This is getting messy. The slim trees now have floating crowns since I painted over their trunks with a sky strip, so I need to redraw the trunks connecting the ridge up into the crowns. The small third tree also has an unwanted blue skirt from the cobalt glaze on its lower foliage, and there's a visible rectangular lighter band in the sky where I repainted the strip.

The sky needs a unifying pass — a full repaint while wet after everything dries, taking the chance to add more atmosphere in Inness style. The ridge currently reads as a hedge or wall with the horizon forming a harsh straight band, so I should make it lighter, bluer, lower, and more varied so the meadow light can pass in front of it. The meadow itself is flat yellow, the pool reads as a plain white blob, and the foreground rust band needs work — overall the middle and right of the composition feel weak and empty.

My plan is to stop doing patchy repairs and instead work in broad, unified passes across whole regions in single sessions, the way Inness would. events.text:
I'm checking the light direction against the shadow cast by the grove, confirming the sun sits upper right behind the trees so the crown highlights and shadow placement stay consistent.

The hard inner contour of the crowns needs softening—I'll add a few small unclipped strokes feathering outward, plus consider sky holes within the foliage for that airy Inness quality, though that needs to wait until the paint dries so it doesn't muddy. Let me step back and assess the whole composition first.

Looking at the whole composition, the left foreground is too flat and dark—it needs warm reflected light, a few grass suggestions, or a dimly lit patch to break up that large featureless olive mass. The grove itself also reads as a flat dark block lacking internal variation.

The rest holds up fairly well—sky is soft with a hint more warmth near the horizon possible, hills are an acceptable flat band, and the meadow transition is fine, though the lit meadow could use subtle darker passages and grass touches to avoid uniformity. Given how risky local repairs have been (my earlier warm scumble attempt turned too bright and had to be covered), I need a careful, low-coverage approach for reworking the shadow field.

I'm thinking a thin raw sienna plus red earth glaze over the dry dark area would deepen it warmly in Inness's style, followed by a few dry-brushed, low-load horizontal strokes of mid-value to catch the canvas weave for broken color texture—testing this on a small patch first. For the grove interior, I'd add small sky holes near the top of the left tree, using a grayish mix close to but slightly darker than the surrounding sky since light seen through foliage usually reads that way, keeping the holes small and clipped to the tree silhouette.

The crowns are still wet, so I'll start with the dry-brush scumble test in the already-dry shadow field instead, leaving the sky holes for after the crowns set.

events.text: Day 149. Calling it finished. It reads as late Inness, more or less: a dark grove held against a warm, misty evening sky, its long shadow lying over the meadow toward us, three young trees backlit by the glow, a far blue ridge, and one small figure with a red shawl right at the edge of light and shade. What's still wrong: the slim crowns are too crisp and round, the far gold strip is a little too insistent, and the grove's leaf fringe on the left is cut out against the sky. I'm not going to push these. Every local fix on dry paint here has left a seam. Lessons for next time: test values small first; a lead-white mixture is opaque at any load; only whole-area wet sessions and soft-edged badger passes have worked; clip everything near what must be kept.

**Evening, the Long Shadow**

I've finished the painting. It's an invented late-summer evening in the manner of Inness's later work. A big oak grove fills the left side, nearly one dark mass against a warm, hazy sky. A single small gap under its canopy shows a strip of far, sunlit field. The low sun sits behind three young trees on the right, and the grove's long shadow lies over the meadow toward us. A small woman in a red shawl stands just where that shadow meets the gold light. She is the only warm accent in an olive, umber and violet-grey setting, beneath a soft blue ridge and a cream-to-mauve sky.

I painted it as he worked: a linen canvas stained with raw umber and sienna, a thin rubbed-in umber lay-in, then many separate sessions over paint that had dried, with glazes and soft blending between them.

Some parts aren't as I wanted. The three young trees are too crisp and round, the far gold strip of field is a little loud, and the grove's leaf edge on the left looks cut out against the sky. I stopped there rather than push further. Fixing small areas on dry paint kept leaving visible seams, and only repainting whole areas wet held together.
